# Project Overview

This project analyses IMDb movie reviews and classifies them as either positive or negative. It covers dataset exploration, data cleaning, text processing, exploratory text analysis, machine-learning model development, model evaluation, and model interpretation using LIME and a coefficient-based SHAP analysis.

The four models compared are Logistic Regression, Multinomial Naive Bayes, Linear Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Ridge-regularised Logistic Regression.

# 1. Setup: Install and Load Packages

This section checks for the packages required for the project and loads them. Package installation is performed only when a package is missing.

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
required_packages <- c(
  "tidyverse", "tidytext", "wordcloud", "RColorBrewer",
  "text2vec", "glmnet", "e1071", "LiblineaR", "pROC", "lime"
)

missing_packages <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]

if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  install.packages(
    missing_packages,
    repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
  )
}

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(wordcloud)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(text2vec)
library(glmnet)
library(e1071)
library(LiblineaR)
library(pROC)
library(lime)
library(Matrix)
```

# 2. Import the Dataset

The IMDb review dataset is imported into R for analysis. Place the CSV file in the same folder as this R Markdown file and make sure its filename matches the one used below.

```{r import-data}
reviews <- read.csv("IMDB Dataset.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dim(reviews)
names(reviews)
head(reviews)
```

# 3. Initial Data Exploration

The dataset is inspected to understand its dimensions, column names, data types, summary statistics, sentiment distribution, missing values, and duplicate reviews.

```{r initial-exploration}
str(reviews)
summary(reviews)

table(reviews$sentiment)
colSums(is.na(reviews))

sum(duplicated(reviews$review))
duplicate_reviews <- reviews[duplicated(reviews$review), ]
head(duplicate_reviews, 10)

table(duplicate_reviews$sentiment)

review_label_check <- aggregate(
  sentiment ~ review,
  data = reviews,
  FUN = function(x) length(unique(x))
)

review_label_check <- review_label_check[
  review_label_check$sentiment > 1,
]

nrow(review_label_check)
```

# 4. Data Cleaning

Duplicate reviews are removed so that each review appears only once. The cleaned dataset is checked for remaining duplicates and empty reviews.

```{r data-cleaning}
reviews_clean <- reviews[!duplicated(reviews$review), ]

dim(reviews_clean)
sum(duplicated(reviews_clean$review))

empty_reviews <- sum(trimws(reviews_clean$review) == "")
empty_reviews

head(reviews_clean$review, 3)
```

# 5. Text Processing and Tokenisation

The review text is prepared for analysis. HTML line-break tags, punctuation, digits, and excess whitespace are removed, and all text is converted to lowercase. Reviews are then tokenised into individual words, and common stop words are removed.

```{r text-processing}
reviews_processed <- reviews_clean

reviews_processed$review <- gsub(
  "<br />", " ", reviews_processed$review
)

head(reviews_processed$review, 3)
glimpse(reviews_processed)

reviews_processed$review <- tolower(reviews_processed$review)

reviews_processed$review <- gsub(
  "[[:punct:]]", " ", reviews_processed$review
)

reviews_processed$review <- gsub(
  "[[:digit:]]", " ", reviews_processed$review
)

reviews_processed$review <- gsub(
  "\\s+", " ", reviews_processed$review
)

reviews_processed$review <- trimws(reviews_processed$review)

reviews_tokens <- reviews_processed %>%
  mutate(review_id = row_number()) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, review) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

head(reviews_tokens, 10)
glimpse(reviews_tokens)
```

# 6. Word Frequency Analysis

Word frequency analysis identifies the most frequently occurring words in the processed IMDb reviews. A bar chart displays the ten most frequent words.

```{r word-frequency}
word_counts <- reviews_tokens %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

head(word_counts)

top_words <- word_counts %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10)

ggplot(top_words, aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Most Frequent Words in IMDb Reviews",
    x = "Words",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 7. Bing Lexicon Sentiment Analysis

The Bing sentiment lexicon assigns words a positive or negative sentiment label. The review tokens are matched with the lexicon to examine sentiment words in the reviews.

Some words in the original lexicon may appear more than once with conflicting sentiment labels. These ambiguous entries are excluded before the final join.

```{r bing-sentiment}
bing_words <- get_sentiments("bing")

sum(duplicated(bing_words$word))

bing_words %>%
  count(word) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

bing_words %>%
  filter(word %in% c("envious", "enviously", "enviousness"))

bing_clean <- bing_words %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  filter(n_distinct(sentiment) == 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  distinct(word, sentiment)

sum(duplicated(bing_clean$word))

review_sentiment_words <- reviews_tokens %>%
  inner_join(bing_clean, by = "word")

head(review_sentiment_words)

sentiment_summary <- review_sentiment_words %>%
  count(sentiment.x, sentiment.y)

sentiment_summary

ggplot(
  sentiment_summary,
  aes(x = sentiment.x, y = n, fill = sentiment.y)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Word Sentiment Across IMDb Reviews",
    x = "IMDb Review Sentiment",
    y = "Word Frequency",
    fill = "Bing Sentiment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 8. Distribution of Review Word Counts

This section counts the words remaining in each review after tokenisation and stop-word removal. A histogram is used to show how review lengths are distributed.

```{r review-word-counts}
reviews_processed$word_count <- stringr::str_count(
  stringr::str_trim(reviews_processed$review),
  "\\S+"
)

review_word_counts <- reviews_tokens %>%
  count(review_id, name = "word_count")

ggplot(review_word_counts, aes(x = word_count)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1,
    fill = "skyblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Review Word Counts",
    x = "Number of Words",
    y = "Number of Reviews"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 9. Positive and Negative Word Frequencies

The most frequent words identified as positive and negative by the Bing lexicon are extracted separately. Bar charts are used to compare the ten most frequent words in each category.

```{r positive-negative-frequencies}
sentiment_word_counts <- review_sentiment_words %>%
  count(word, sentiment.y, sort = TRUE)

head(sentiment_word_counts, 10)

positive_words <- sentiment_word_counts %>%
  filter(sentiment.y == "positive") %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10)

head(positive_words)

negative_words <- sentiment_word_counts %>%
  filter(sentiment.y == "negative") %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 10)

head(negative_words)

ggplot(positive_words, aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "forestgreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Positive Words in IMDb Reviews",
    x = "Words",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(negative_words, aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Negative Words in IMDb Reviews",
    x = "Words",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 10. Total Positive and Negative Word Counts

The total number of positive and negative words matched by the Bing lexicon is calculated and displayed in a bar chart.

```{r total-sentiment-words}
review_sentiment_count <- review_sentiment_words %>%
  count(sentiment.y, sort = TRUE)

head(review_sentiment_count)

ggplot(
  review_sentiment_count,
  aes(x = sentiment.y, y = n, fill = sentiment.y)
) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Positive vs Negative Words in IMDb Reviews",
    x = "Sentiment",
    y = "Word Count"
  ) +

```

# 11. Compare Bing Word Sentiment Across Review Categories

This comparison examines how many positive and negative lexicon words occur in reviews labelled positive or negative in the original dataset. Percentages are calculated within each original review sentiment category.

```{r sentiment-comparison}
review_comparison <- review_sentiment_words %>%
  count(sentiment.x, sentiment.y)

review_comparison

review_comparison %>%
  group_by(sentiment.x) %>%
  mutate(percentage = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))
```

# 12. TF-IDF Analysis

Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) is used to identify words that are relatively important to individual reviews. Words that occur frequently in a particular review but less frequently across the collection can receive higher TF-IDF scores.

The analysis calculates TF-IDF scores, summarises the average score for each word, and filters out words that occur in fewer than ten reviews before selecting the top ten.

```{r tf-idf}
tf_idf_words <- reviews_tokens %>%
  count(review_id, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  bind_tf_idf(word, review_id, n)

glimpse(tf_idf_words)
head(tf_idf_words, 10)

tf_idf_words %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf)) %>%
  select(word, review_id, n, tf, idf, tf_idf) %>%
  head(10)

top_tfidf_words <- tf_idf_words %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  summarise(mean_tf_idf = mean(tf_idf), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_tf_idf)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

top_tfidf_words

ggplot(
  top_tfidf_words,
  aes(x = reorder(word, mean_tf_idf), y = mean_tf_idf)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Words by TF-IDF Score",
    x = "Words",
    y = "Mean TF-IDF"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

tf_idf_words %>%
  arrange(desc(tf_idf)) %>%
  head(30)

names(tf_idf_words)

tf_idf_summary <- tf_idf_words %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  summarise(mean_tf_idf = mean(tf_idf), .groups = "drop")

tf_idf_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_tf_idf)) %>%
  head(30)

tf_idf_words %>%
  filter(word %in% c("trivialboring", "barwork", "someplaces")) %>%
  select(review_id, word, tf_idf) %>%
  head(10)

reviews_processed[18633, "review"]
reviews_processed[23538, "review"]

tf_idf_summary <- tf_idf_words %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  summarise(
    document_frequency = n_distinct(review_id),
    mean_tf_idf = mean(tf_idf),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(document_frequency >= 10) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_tf_idf))

top_tfidf_words <- tf_idf_summary %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

top_tfidf_words

ggplot(
  top_tfidf_words,
  aes(x = reorder(word, mean_tf_idf), y = mean_tf_idf)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Words by TF-IDF Score",
    x = "Words",
    y = "Mean TF-IDF Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 13. Word Clouds

Word clouds provide a visual representation of frequently occurring positive and negative words. The size of each word reflects its frequency in the corresponding sentiment category.

```{r word-clouds}
positive_wordcloud <- sentiment_word_counts %>%
  filter(sentiment.y == "positive") %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

head(positive_wordcloud, 10)

wordcloud(
  words = positive_wordcloud$word,
  freq = positive_wordcloud$n,
  max.words = 100,
  random.order = FALSE,
  colors = brewer.pal(8, "Dark2")
)

negative_wordcloud <- sentiment_word_counts %>%
  filter(sentiment.y == "negative") %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

head(negative_wordcloud, 10)

wordcloud(
  words = negative_wordcloud$word,
  freq = negative_wordcloud$n,
  max.words = 100,
  random.order = FALSE,
  colors = brewer.pal(8, "Reds")[5:8]
)
```

# 14. Heatmap of Positive and Negative Words

A heatmap is created to compare the frequencies of the ten most frequent positive and negative words identified by the Bing lexicon. The colour intensity represents word frequency.

```{r sentiment-heatmap}
heatmap_words <- sentiment_word_counts %>%
  group_by(sentiment.y) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 10) %>%
  ungroup()

head(heatmap_words, 20)

ggplot(
  heatmap_words,
  aes(x = sentiment.y, y = reorder(word, n), fill = n)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Heatmap of Top Positive and Negative Words",
    x = "Sentiment",
    y = "Word",
    fill = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 15. Prepare Data for Machine Learning

The processed reviews are divided into training and testing datasets. A fixed random seed is used to make the split reproducible. The split is performed within each sentiment category to retain the class balance.

```{r train-test-split}
set.seed(123)

reviews_model <- reviews_processed %>%
  mutate(review_id = row_number())

train_data <- reviews_model %>%
  group_by(sentiment) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 0.8) %>%
  ungroup()

test_data <- reviews_model %>%
  filter(!review_id %in% train_data$review_id)

dim(train_data)
dim(test_data)

table(train_data$sentiment)
table(test_data$sentiment)
```

# 16. Create the Training Vocabulary and Document-Term Matrices

The training reviews are tokenised, and stop words are removed. A vocabulary is created and pruned to remove terms that occur too rarely or in too large a proportion of documents. The vocabulary is then used to create document-term matrices for the training and testing data.

The test data uses the training vocabulary so that both matrices contain the same features.

```{r document-term-matrices}
tokens_train <- word_tokenizer(train_data$review)

tokens_train <- lapply(tokens_train, function(words) {
  words[!words %in% stop_words$word]
})

it_train <- itoken(
  tokens_train,
  progressbar = FALSE
)

vocab <- create_vocabulary(it_train)

vocab <- prune_vocabulary(
  vocab,
  term_count_min = 5,
  doc_proportion_max = 0.5
)

vocab

vectorizer <- vocab_vectorizer(vocab)

dtm_train <- create_dtm(
  it_train,
  vectorizer
)

dim(dtm_train)

tokens_test <- word_tokenizer(test_data$review)

tokens_test <- lapply(tokens_test, function(words) {
  words[!words %in% stop_words$word]
})

it_test <- itoken(
  tokens_test,
  progressbar = FALSE
)

dtm_test <- create_dtm(
  it_test,
  vectorizer
)

dim(dtm_test)

y_train <- ifelse(train_data$sentiment == "positive", 1, 0)
y_test <- ifelse(test_data$sentiment == "positive", 1, 0)

table(y_train)
table(y_test)
```

# 17. Logistic Regression Model

A LASSO-regularised logistic regression model is trained using the training document-term matrix. The model predicts the probability that each test review belongs to the positive sentiment class. A probability threshold of 0.5 is used to assign predicted classes.

```{r logistic-regression}
set.seed(123)

logistic_model <- glmnet(
  x = dtm_train,
  y = y_train,
  family = "binomial",
  alpha = 1,
  nlambda = 20,
  maxit = 10000
)

print(logistic_model)

length(logistic_model$lambda)
logistic_model$lambda

logistic_lambda <- logistic_model$lambda[7]

logistic_pred <- predict(
  logistic_model,
  newx = dtm_test,
  s = logistic_lambda,
  type = "response"
)

head(logistic_pred)

logistic_class <- ifelse(logistic_pred >= 0.5, 1, 0)

head(logistic_class)

logistic_accuracy <- mean(logistic_class == y_test)
logistic_accuracy

logistic_cm <- table(
  Actual = y_test,
  Predicted = logistic_class
)

logistic_cm

precision <- 4444 / (4444 + 943)
recall <- 4444 / (4444 + 533)

f1_score <- 2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall)

precision
recall
f1_score

logistic_result <- data.frame(
  Model = "Logistic Regression",
  Accuracy = logistic_accuracy,
  Precision = precision,
  Recall = recall,
  F1 = f1_score
)

logistic_result

write.csv(
  logistic_result,
  "logistic_regression_results.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

# 18. Naive Bayes Model

A Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier is implemented using word counts from the training document-term matrix. Laplace smoothing is applied to avoid zero word probabilities. The model calculates class scores for the test reviews and predicts the class with the higher score.

```{r naive-bayes}
negative_counts <- Matrix::colSums(
  dtm_train[y_train == 0, , drop = FALSE]
)

positive_counts <- Matrix::colSums(
  dtm_train[y_train == 1, , drop = FALSE]
)

smoothing <- 1

negative_prob <- (negative_counts + smoothing) /
  (sum(negative_counts) + smoothing * ncol(dtm_train))

positive_prob <- (positive_counts + smoothing) /
  (sum(positive_counts) + smoothing * ncol(dtm_train))

head(positive_prob)
head(negative_prob)

prior_negative <- mean(y_train == 0)
prior_positive <- mean(y_train == 1)

prior_positive
prior_negative

negative_score <- log(prior_negative) +
  dtm_test %*% log(negative_prob)

positive_score <- log(prior_positive) +
  dtm_test %*% log(positive_prob)

naive_bayes_pred <- ifelse(
  positive_score > negative_score,
  1,
  0
)

head(naive_bayes_pred)

naive_bayes_cm <- table(
  Actual = y_test,
  Predicted = naive_bayes_pred
)

naive_bayes_cm

naive_bayes_accuracy <- mean(naive_bayes_pred == y_test)

naive_bayes_precision <- 4174 / (4174 + 618)
naive_bayes_recall <- 4174 / (4174 + 803)

naive_bayes_f1 <- 2 * (
  naive_bayes_precision * naive_bayes_recall
) / (
  naive_bayes_precision + naive_bayes_recall
)

naive_bayes_accuracy
naive_bayes_precision
naive_bayes_recall
naive_bayes_f1

naive_bayes_result <- data.frame(
  Model = "Naive Bayes",
  Accuracy = naive_bayes_accuracy,
  Precision = naive_bayes_precision,
  Recall = naive_bayes_recall,
  F1 = naive_bayes_f1
)

naive_bayes_result
```

# 19. Linear Support Vector Machine Model

A Linear Support Vector Machine is trained using the 3,000 most frequent features in the training data. Restricting the number of features helps reduce memory requirements. The trained model is then used to predict sentiment labels for the test reviews.

```{r linear-svm}
pkg_available <- requireNamespace("LiblineaR", quietly = TRUE)
print(pkg_available)

feature_frequency <- Matrix::colSums(dtm_train)

top_features <- names(
  sort(feature_frequency, decreasing = TRUE)
)[1:3000]

dtm_train_svm <- dtm_train[, top_features]
dtm_test_svm <- dtm_test[, top_features]

dim(dtm_train_svm)
dim(dtm_test_svm)

set.seed(123)

svm_model <- LiblineaR(
  data = dtm_train_svm,
  target = y_train,
  type = 1,
  cost = 1,
  bias = TRUE
)

class(svm_model)

svm_pred <- predict(
  svm_model,
  dtm_test_svm
)

head(svm_pred)
class(svm_pred)
dim(svm_pred)
str(svm_pred)

svm_pred_class <- svm_pred$predictions

head(svm_pred_class)

svm_cm <- table(
  Actual = y_test,
  Predicted = svm_pred_class
)

svm_cm

svm_accuracy <- sum(diag(svm_cm)) / sum(svm_cm)
svm_precision <- 4351 / (4351 + 715)
svm_recall <- 4351 / (4351 + 626)

svm_f1 <- 2 * (
  svm_precision * svm_recall
) / (
  svm_precision + svm_recall
)

svm_accuracy
svm_precision
svm_recall
svm_f1

svm_result <- data.frame(
  Model = "Linear SVM",
  Accuracy = svm_accuracy,
  Precision = svm_precision,
  Recall = svm_recall,
  F1 = svm_f1
)

svm_result
```

# 20. Ridge-Regularised Logistic Regression Model

A logistic regression model with L2 (Ridge) regularisation is trained using `glmnet` with `alpha = 0`. The model predicts positive-class probabilities for the test reviews, which are converted into class predictions using a threshold of 0.5.

```{r ridge-model}
set.seed(123)

ridge_model <- glmnet(
  x = dtm_train,
  y = y_train,
  family = "binomial",
  alpha = 0,
  nlambda = 30,
  maxit = 100000
)

class(ridge_model)

ridge_lambda <- ridge_model$lambda[15]

ridge_prob <- predict(
  ridge_model,
  newx = dtm_test,
  type = "response",
  s = ridge_lambda
)

head(ridge_model$lambda)
length(ridge_model$lambda)
tail(ridge_model$lambda)

ridge_pred <- ifelse(ridge_prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

head(ridge_prob)
length(ridge_pred)

ridge_cm <- table(
  Actual = y_test,
  Predicted = ridge_pred
)

ridge_cm

ridge_accuracy <- sum(diag(ridge_cm)) / sum(ridge_cm)
ridge_precision <- 4455 / (4455 + 643)
ridge_recall <- 4455 / (4455 + 522)

ridge_f1 <- 2 * (
  ridge_precision * ridge_recall
) / (
  ridge_precision + ridge_recall
)

ridge_accuracy
ridge_precision
ridge_recall
ridge_f1

ridge_result <- data.frame(
  Model = "Ridge classifier",
  Accuracy = ridge_accuracy,
  Precision = ridge_precision,
  Recall = ridge_recall,
  F1 = ridge_f1
)

ridge_result
```

# 21. Model Performance Comparison

The performance metrics from the four models are combined into one table. A grouped bar chart compares accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score across the models.

```{r model-comparison}
model_comparison <- bind_rows(
  logistic_result,
  naive_bayes_result,
  svm_result,
  ridge_result
)

model_comparison

write.csv(
  model_comparison,
  "model_comparison.csv",
  row.names = FALSE
)

model_comparison_long <- model_comparison %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Score"
  )

ggplot(
  model_comparison_long,
  aes(x = Model, y = Score, fill = Metric)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Machine Learning Model Performance Comparison",
    x = "Machine Learning Models",
    y = "Performance Score",
    fill = "Evaluation Metric"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1)
  )
```

# 22. Confusion Matrix Visualisations

Confusion matrices show the number of correct and incorrect predictions made by each model. The visualisations compare actual sentiment labels with predicted sentiment labels.

```{r confusion-matrices}
logistic_cm_df <- as.data.frame(logistic_cm)

ggplot(
  logistic_cm_df,
  aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Freq)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Logistic Regression Confusion Matrix",
    x = "Predicted Sentiment",
    y = "Actual Sentiment",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

naive_bayes_plot <- as.data.frame(as.table(naive_bayes_cm))
names(naive_bayes_plot) <- c("Actual", "Predicted", "Count")

ggplot(
  naive_bayes_plot,
  aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Count)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Naive Bayes Confusion Matrix",
    x = "Predicted Sentiment",
    y = "Actual Sentiment",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

svm_plot <- as.data.frame(as.table(svm_cm))
names(svm_plot) <- c("Actual", "Predicted", "Count")

ggplot(
  svm_plot,
  aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Count)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Linear SVM Confusion Matrix",
    x = "Predicted Sentiment",
    y = "Actual Sentiment",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ridge_plot <- as.data.frame(as.table(ridge_cm))
names(ridge_plot) <- c("Actual", "Predicted", "Count")

ggplot(
  ridge_plot,
  aes(x = Predicted, y = Actual, fill = Count)
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), size = 6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Ridge Classifier Confusion Matrix",
    x = "Predicted Sentiment",
    y = "Actual Sentiment",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 23. ROC Curve and AUC Analysis

Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves show the trade-off between the true positive rate and false positive rate at different classification thresholds. The Area Under the Curve (AUC) summarises the model's ability to distinguish between the two sentiment classes.

For Logistic Regression, the same lambda value used for its class predictions is used here so that the ROC analysis corresponds to the reported classification model.

```{r roc-analysis}
logistic_prob <- as.numeric(
  predict(
    logistic_model,
    newx = dtm_test,
    type = "response",
    s = logistic_lambda
  )
)

head(logistic_prob)

logistic_roc <- pROC::roc(
  response = y_test,
  predictor = logistic_prob,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  direction = "<"
)

logistic_auc <- pROC::auc(logistic_roc)
logistic_auc

plot(
  logistic_roc,
  main = "Logistic Regression ROC Curve",
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2
)

abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")

naive_bayes_score <- as.numeric(
  as.matrix(positive_score - negative_score)
)

naive_bayes_prob <- plogis(naive_bayes_score)

naive_bayes_roc <- pROC::roc(
  response = y_test,
  predictor = naive_bayes_prob,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  direction = "<"
)

naive_bayes_auc <- pROC::auc(naive_bayes_roc)
naive_bayes_auc

plot(
  naive_bayes_roc,
  main = "Naive Bayes ROC Curve",
  col = "darkgreen",
  lwd = 2
)

abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")

svm_score_obj <- predict(
  svm_model,
  dtm_test_svm,
  decisionValues = TRUE
)

str(svm_score_obj)

svm_score <- svm_score_obj$decisionValues[, "1"]

svm_roc <- pROC::roc(
  response = y_test,
  predictor = svm_score_obj$decisionValues[, "0"],
  levels = c(0, 1)
)

svm_auc <- pROC::auc(svm_roc)
svm_auc

head(svm_score_obj$decisionValues)
colnames(svm_score_obj$decisionValues)

plot(
  svm_roc,
  main = "SVM ROC Curve",
  col = "purple",
  lwd = 2
)

abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "red")

ridge_roc <- pROC::roc(
  response = y_test,
  predictor = as.numeric(ridge_prob),
  levels = c(0, 1),
  direction = "<"
)

ridge_auc <- pROC::auc(ridge_roc)
ridge_auc

plot(
  ridge_roc,
  main = "Ridge Classifier ROC Curve",
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)

abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2, col = "blue")
```

# 24. Combined ROC Curve Comparison

The ROC curves of all four models are plotted together to compare their discrimination performance. The legend displays the AUC values obtained in the analysis.

```{r combined-roc}
plot(
  logistic_roc,
  main = "ROC Curve Comparison of All Models",
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2
)

plot(naive_bayes_roc, add = TRUE, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
plot(svm_roc, add = TRUE, col = "purple", lwd = 2)
plot(ridge_roc, add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)

legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c(
    paste0("Logistic Regression (AUC = ", round(as.numeric(logistic_auc), 4), ")"),

    paste0("SVM (AUC = ", round(as.numeric(svm_auc), 4), ")"),

  ),
  col = c("blue", "darkgreen", "purple", "red"),
  lwd = 2,
  cex = 0.7
)
```

# 26. LIME Model Interpretation

Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) is used to explain an individual prediction made by the Ridge-regularised logistic regression model. A custom prediction interface converts new review text into a document-term matrix and returns the model's predicted probabilities for the negative and positive classes.

The first review in the test dataset is selected as the example to explain.

```{r lime-analysis}
ridge_classifier <- list(
  model = ridge_model,
  vectorizer = vectorizer
)

class(ridge_classifier) <- "ridge_classifier"

model_type.ridge_classifier <- function(x, ...) {
  "classification"
}

predict_model.ridge_classifier <- function(x, newdata, ...) {
  tokens <- text2vec::word_tokenizer(newdata)

  tokens <- lapply(tokens, function(words) {
    words[!words %in% tidytext::stop_words$word]
  })

  it <- text2vec::itoken(
    tokens,
    progressbar = FALSE
  )

  dtm <- text2vec::create_dtm(
    it,
    x$vectorizer
  )

  probabilities <- as.numeric(
    predict(
      x$model,
      newx = dtm,
      type = "response",
      s = x$model$lambda[15]
    )
  )

  data.frame(
    negative = 1 - probabilities,
    positive = probabilities
  )
}

explainer <- lime::lime(
  x = train_data$review,
  model = ridge_classifier,
  feature_type = "text"
)

sample_review <- test_data$review[1]

explanation <- lime::explain(
  x = sample_review,
  explainer = explainer,
  n_labels = 1,
  n_features = 10,
  n_permutations = 500
)

plot_features(explanation)
```

# 27. Coefficient-Based SHAP Analysis

This section calculates SHAP-style feature contributions for the Ridge-regularised logistic regression model. The contribution for each feature is calculated from the difference between the selected test review's feature value and the training-data background mean, multiplied by the corresponding model coefficient.

The resulting values represent contributions on the model's linear predictor (log-odds) scale. Their signs indicate the direction of the contribution to the model output, while their absolute values indicate contribution magnitude.

```{r shap-analysis}
ridge_coef <- as.matrix(
  coef(ridge_model, s = ridge_model$lambda[15])
)

feature_names <- colnames(dtm_train)

ridge_beta <- as.numeric(
  ridge_coef[feature_names, 1]
)

names(ridge_beta) <- feature_names

background_mean <- Matrix::colMeans(dtm_train)

sample_dtm <- dtm_test[1, , drop = FALSE]

sample_values <- as.numeric(as.matrix(sample_dtm))

shap_contributions <- (
  sample_values - background_mean
) * ridge_beta

shap_results <- data.frame(
  Feature = feature_names,
  SHAP_Value = as.numeric(shap_contributions)
)

shap_results <- shap_results[
  order(abs(shap_results$SHAP_Value), decreasing = TRUE),
]

head(shap_results, 10)

ggplot(
  shap_results[1:10, ],
  aes(
    x = reorder(Feature, abs(SHAP_Value)),
    y = abs(SHAP_Value)
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Features by SHAP Importance",
    x = "Features",
    y = "Absolute SHAP Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# 28. Project Conclusion

This project explored and processed IMDb movie reviews, examined word-level sentiment patterns, and developed four machine-learning models for binary sentiment classification. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrices, and ROC-AUC.

LIME was used to explain an individual prediction, while a coefficient-based SHAP analysis was used to examine feature contributions for a selected review. The model comparison and interpretation results can be used to discuss the strengths and limitations of the approaches.

# 29. Important Notes and Limitations

- The Bing lexicon analysis is based only on words present in the lexicon. It does not fully understand context, negation, sarcasm, or phrases.
- The Naive Bayes model in this script is implemented manually using word counts and Laplace smoothing.
- The SVM model uses the 3,000 most frequent training features to reduce memory use.
- The Ridge model is a logistic regression model with L2 regularisation (`alpha = 0` in `glmnet`).
- The SHAP-style calculation shown here is a coefficient-based linear-model contribution calculation using the training feature means as the background. It relies on a simplified feature contribution approach and should be described accordingly.
- The reported precision, recall, and F1 calculations use the confusion-matrix counts shown in the original analysis. If the model or dataset changes, these values should be recalculated from the corresponding confusion matrix.
